report.summary: Chunk 6 of 6 for ledger.py: defines resolve_by_effect, intents_for_trace, events, _hydrate, close, __enter__, __exit__, and _row_to_intent; includes docstring claims and defensive comments.
risks: resolve_by_effect return type | medium | Docstring says returns list[Intent] but may return list of dicts if _hydrate fails; verify _hydrate always returns Intent.
intents_for_trace fallback | low | Returns [] on empty trace_id but also on 'no such column' error; could mask other OperationalErrors that contain 'no such column' in message.
_row_to_intent trace_id fallback | low | Uses row.keys() check; if sqlite3.Row.keys() is expensive or not present in older Python, could fail.

handoff.purpose: Defines query methods (resolve_by_effect, intents_for_trace, events), lifecycle methods (close, __enter__, __exit__), internal helper _hydrate, and standalone function _row_to_intent.

symbols.name: resolve_by_effect
symbols.note: Method on SpineLedger; queries intents by effect_key, returns list of Intent objects.

claims.text: Every intent recorded under ``effect_key``, oldest first.
claims.why: Query uses WHERE effect_key = ? ORDER BY id, which returns oldest first (id is monotonically increasing).
Function only executes a SELECT query; no INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.

claims.text: It returns a list because retries legitimately reuse a key
claims.why: Claim about why list is returned; no evidence in chunk that retries reuse keys, but returning list is consistent with that possibility.

claims.text: Every intent recorded under one ``trace_id``, oldest first.
claims.why: Query uses WHERE trace_id = ? ORDER BY id, oldest first.

claims.text: THE JOIN. This is the ledger's half of "what did that run actually do" -- the other halves are the loop ledger's ``trace_id`` and the bridge records', and all three carry the same value so one grep spans them.
claims.why: Refers to external components (loop ledger, bridge records) not present in this chunk.

claims.text: Returns ``[]`` rather than raising on a pre-v2 database that has no such column.
claims.why: Code catches sqlite3.OperationalError with 'no such column' and returns [].

claims.text: That is the correct answer, not a swallowed error: a v1 file provably contains no traced rows, so "no intents under this trace" is true
claims.why: Asserts v1 file has no trace_id column and no traced rows; not verifiable from this chunk alone.

claims.text: The full append-only transition history for one intent.
claims.why: Query selects all rows from intent_events for given intent_id, ordered by id (append-only).

claims.text: DEFENSIVE, and not merely belt-and-braces: a read_only ledger skips _migrate entirely (mode=ro cannot ALTER), so a reader opened against an un-migrated v1 file gets rows with no trace_id column at all. Asking the ROW what it has keeps that reader working instead of turning "this database is older than you" into an IndexError.
claims.why: Code checks 'trace_id' in row.keys() and defaults to None, preventing KeyError if column missing.

observations.what: resolve_by_effect and intents_for_trace both return lists of Intent via _hydrate; _hydrate calls _terminal_event which is not defined in this chunk.
intents_for_trace catches OperationalError with substring check; may catch errors other than missing column if message contains 'no such column'.
_row_to_intent uses row.keys() to check for trace_id; assumes keys() returns a collection supporting 'in' operator; could be slow or unavailable in older sqlite3 versions.
events function constructs IntentEvent objects; IntentEvent class not defined in this chunk.
close method catches sqlite3.Error but does not log or handle; may silently swallow errors.
